name: Quantum phase estimation (statevector)
summary: Simulate textbook quantum phase estimation for a given eigenphase and read off the estimate, its probability and seeded counts.
description:
Runs textbook quantum phase estimation as a statevector simulation of the gate sequence: Hadamards on the counting register, the controlled-U^(2^j) phase kickback against an eigenstate with eigenphase phi, and an inverse quantum Fourier transform. The output distribution is the Born rule applied to the final state, not a formula for what it should be.

Use it to see how the number of counting qubits sets the resolution, to check that a dyadic phase is recovered with certainty, and to inspect the spread of outcomes for a phase the register cannot represent exactly. Pure Python: no optional dependencies.
useCases: Show that a phase k/2^n is estimated exactly with probability 1
Inspect the outcome distribution for a phase between grid points
Choose the number of counting qubits needed for a target precision

inputs.name: phase
inputs.description: Eigenphase phi in [0, 1); the eigenvalue is exp(2 pi i phi).

inputs.name: counting_qubits
inputs.description: Size n of the counting register; the resolution is 2^-n.

inputs.name: shots
inputs.description: Measurement samples drawn from the exact distribution.

outputs.name: estimated_phase
outputs.description: m / 2^n for the most probable outcome m.

outputs.name: success_probability
outputs.description: Exact probability of that most probable outcome.

outputs.name: phase_error
outputs.description: Distance on the circle between the estimate and the true phase.

outputs.name: top_outcomes
outputs.description: The eight most probable outcomes with their exact probabilities.

changes: First catalog release, wrapping the SDK's existing statevector phase-estimation simulation.

environment.resources: 16 counting qubits: under 1 s and <100 MB; 12 or fewer: well under 0.1 s. Pure Python.

example.code:
import json
from ketqat_runner import catalog

record = catalog.run("quantum-phase-estimation@1.0.0", seed=11, phase=0.3125, counting_qubits=4, shots=500)
result = record.result
print(json.dumps({
    "status": record.status,
    "measured_integer": result["measured_integer"],
    "estimated_phase": result["estimated_phase"],
    "success_probability": round(result["success_probability"], 9),
    "counts": result["counts"],
}))

verified.platform: macOS-27.0.1-arm64-arm-64bit (maintainer run of python/tests/test_catalog_examples.py; not yet run by CI)

sampleResult.summary: Phase 0.3 is not representable with 6 counting qubits: the most probable estimate is 0.296875 (integer 19) with probability 0.8752; the remaining probability spreads over neighbouring outcomes.

assumptions: The second register is prepared in an exact eigenstate of U, so the controlled powers act only as phases on the counting register.
scope: Eigenphases in [0, 1) and 1 to 16 counting qubits.
Exact output distribution plus seeded sampling of measurement outcomes.
limitations: The unitary U and its eigenstate are not simulated; only the eigenphase enters, so the cost of implementing controlled-U^(2^j) is not represented.
Only the eight most probable outcomes are copied into the result; the full 2^n distribution is not stored.
Tested on macOS and Linux only; Windows is untested.

origin.statement: Phase estimation is due to Kitaev (1995) and was given its standard circuit form by Cleve, Ekert, Macchiavello and Mosca (1998). KetQat wrote the pure-Python statevector simulation in this SDK (phase_estimation.py and fourier.py), its validation tests and this catalog entry. KetQat did not invent the method.

validation.description: A phase k/2^n is estimated as exactly k with probability 1 for every k at n = 1..8.
For non-dyadic phases the full simulated distribution matches the analytic Fejer-kernel form P(m) = sin^2(pi 2^n d) / (4^n sin^2(pi d)), d = phi - m/2^n, to 1e-12.
The example code is executed verbatim in a clean virtual environment with the base install only.
